problem: Existing LLM-based navigation targets single robots or homogeneous teams, and multi-robot systems use centralized planners or hand-designed coordination and communication. None automatically generates or adapts a collaboration strategy for heterogeneous robots with different skills.
motivation: Real large-scale search tasks need robots to exploit complementary skills (speed, manipulation arm, high-resolution camera). The strategy must also change when a robot's condition changes mid-mission, for example when its battery runs out. LLM knowledge and dialogue ability make it possible to generate the strategy automatically from robot skill descriptions.
key_idea: Each robot shares its skill and condition description, one randomly chosen robot prompts an LLM to generate a team collaboration strategy (roles, communication, task split), and each robot then plans decentrally with an LLM-based local planner. The strategy is regenerated when a robot's condition changes.
insight: The LLM-generated strategy improves efficiency mainly by distributing search work and matching roles to skills. With three heterogeneous agents, episode time falls by 44.28% relative to the uncoordinated SayNav baseline (537.43 s to 299.45 s). Ablations show that feedback and summary in the local planner prompt matter, since SR falls from 90 to 84 without feedback and to 78 without both. A human-refined strategy performs about the same as the LLM one, so the generated strategy is near what a human would write. Regenerating the strategy after a battery failure raises SR from 88 to 92.
method: Top-level global planner: builds a prompt from the team task statement (with CoT), the robot skills and conditions (shared among robots), a strategy request and tips, and asks the LLM for the collaboration strategy (roles, communication mechanism, task distribution). It is regenerated when a robot's condition changes.

Middle-level local planner: each robot's LLM generates short-term step-by-step plans as compositions of behavior functions such as NavigationTo and OpenObject. The dynamic prompt contains feedback on the previous plan, a task-progress summary (memory), the local scene graph, and messages from other robots. It handles both in-room search and room-to-room transitions with no heuristic rules.

Graph generator: builds and expands a local 3D scene graph from RGBD observations, extended from SayNav. It is augmented with information from teammates' messages, such as which rooms have been explored, and a subgraph around the agent is converted to text.
Bottom-level action planner: maps each planned step to primitive actions, using an A* oracle planner for navigation and oracle manipulation actions.
Decentralized communication: robots share information during navigation, so each robot's plan is continuously updated from teammates' findings and progress.

setting.observation: RGBD images and semantic segmentation, with robot-dependent quality (normal or high-resolution camera); converted into a local 3D scene graph
setting.action_space: high-level behavior functions (NavigationTo, OpenObject, etc.) mapped to primitive actions (turn-left, turn-right, move-forward, stop, look-around, open/close) by an oracle A* planner and oracle manipulation
setting.privileged: oracle A* navigation planner and oracle manipulation actions

numbers.eval_set_note: custom benchmark of 50 ProcTHOR episodes (houses with 3-10 rooms, 3 target objects each)
numbers.extra: oracle A* navigation and oracle manipulation; SPL not used

numbers_note: Custom benchmark, not an established one. Other own rows in Tables 1-4 (2-agent case 2, adaptive strategy, human-refined, ablations) are omitted. The adaptive-strategy row has SR 92.0 and 319.31 s.
results: With three heterogeneous agents, SayCoNav reaches SR 90.0 and 299.45 s, against 537.43 s for the SayNav baseline (44.28% faster). With three homogeneous agents it takes 195.98 s versus 252.17 s for SayNav. Adapting the strategy after a battery failure raises SR from 88 to 92 and cuts time from 331.37 s to 319.31 s.
limitations: Fails when tasks need tight coordination among robots with different skills, such as opening a box or fridge and detecting a tiny object inside; this caused most failures.
LLM hallucinations remain, such as ignoring an unexplored door or doing redundant searches.
Only simulation with oracle navigation and manipulation on a small 50-episode custom benchmark; no real robots; compared only against a SayNav-based baseline.
